name: LM1084IS-3.3_NOPB
title: 5 A low-dropout positive regulator, 3.3 V, 5.0 V and adjustable
summary: The LM1084 is a 5 A positive linear regulator with an NPN pass transistor, dropping 1.3 V typical and 1.5 V at most at full load. It comes as fixed 3.3 V and 5.0 V parts and an adjustable part with a 1.25 V reference, in TO-263 and TO-220, with the LM317 pin order. Current limiting and thermal shutdown are built in; it needs a tantalum or aluminium output capacitor for stability. LM1084IS-3.3/NOPB is the 3.3 V part in TO-263, in tubes of 45.

circuits.title: 1.2 V to 15 V adjustable regulator
circuits.description: The adjustable part set by a 121 Ω resistor from OUTPUT to ADJ and a 5 kΩ potentiometer from ADJ to ground; turning the potentiometer moves the output between about 1.2 V and 15 V, following VOUT = 1.25 V × (1 + R2/R1). A 10 µF tantalum holds the output stable. The 10 µF input capacitor is only called for when the regulator sits far from the supply's filter capacitors.

parts.note: needed when the part is far from the filter capacitors

circuits.title: Fixed-output regulator with line resistance to the load
circuits.description: A fixed-output part feeding a remote load through wiring modelled as Rt1 in the supply lead and Rt2 in the return. The load sees VOUT less the drop IL × (Rt1 + Rt2); running the load's positive lead straight to OUTPUT and its negative lead straight to the GND pin keeps that drop out of the regulation.

circuits.title: Adjustable regulator wired for best load regulation
circuits.description: The adjustable part with the top of R1 taken right at OUTPUT, so the drop in the supply lead Rt1 is not multiplied by the divider, and the bottom of R2 returned at the load's ground end so that the return drop in Rt2 is sensed. The load voltage is VREF × (R1 + R2)/R1 − IL × Rt1.

circuits.title: Basic adjustable regulator
circuits.description: The adjustable part holds 1.25 V (VREF) across R1, from OUTPUT to ADJ; the current that sets flows on down through R2, and the drop on R2 adds to VREF to make the output. The small ADJ current adds IADJ × R2. 10 µF at the input and a 10 µF tantalum at the output.

circuits.title: Adjustable regulator with protection diode
circuits.description: An adjustable regulator with a 10 µF capacitor on ADJ and 150 µF on the output. An optional 1N4002 from OUTPUT back to INPUT carries the output capacitor's discharge if the input is shorted, which matters with a very large output capacitor (1000 µF or more).

circuits.title: Adjustable regulator set to 5 V
circuits.description: The adjustable part set to 5 V at up to 5 A by a 121 Ω / 365 Ω pair of 1 % resistors, from an input of 6.5 V or more. A 10 µF capacitor sits at the input and a 10 µF tantalum at the output; the output one is needed for stability.
notes: VIN ≥ 6.5 V; output 5 V at 5 A.

circuits.title: 5 V regulator with shutdown
circuits.description: The 5 V adjustable circuit with a 2N3904 from ADJ to ground. A high TTL level turns the transistor on, ADJ is pulled to ground and the output falls to about 1.25 V; a low level leaves the transistor off and the regulator runs normally. The base is fed through 1 kΩ with 1 kΩ to ground.

circuits.title: Battery charger
circuits.description: The adjustable part charging a battery at VOUT through a sense resistor RS. The divider R1/R2 is taken from the battery side of RS, so the regulator holds a float voltage and the charge current falls off as the battery comes up to it. The charge current is IF = (VOUT − 1.25 × (1 + R2/R1)) / (−RS × (1 + R2/R1)).

circuits.title: Fixed regulator raised by a resistor in the ground lead
circuits.description: The 5.0 V fixed part with a 1 kΩ potentiometer from its GND pin to ground. The pin's quiescent current (5 mA typical) through the potentiometer lifts the GND pin, and the output rises by the same amount, giving 5 V to 10 V from an input above 12 V. An optional 10 µF across the potentiometer improves ripple rejection; 10 µF at the input, 100 µF at the output.
notes: VIN > 12 V; output 5 V to 10 V.

circuits.title: Regulator with reference
circuits.description: The 5.0 V fixed part standing on an LM136-5 reference diode in its ground lead. The pin's quiescent current biases the reference, holding the GND pin at 5 V, which is also brought out as a reference rail, and the output sits 5 V higher at 10 V. Input above 11.5 V, 10 µF at the input and 100 µF at the output.
notes: VIN > 11.5 V.

circuits.title: High-current lamp driver protection
circuits.description: A 12 V, 5 A lamp in the input lead from a 15 V supply, with ADJ grounded. A TTL or CMOS level drives a pair of NPN transistors that drag OUTPUT down to some tenths of a volt, putting the regulator into current limit; releasing the input lets the lamp current return to its normal value. The scheme protects the lamp at switch-on.

circuits.title: Battery-backed regulated supply
circuits.description: Two 5.0 V fixed parts with their outputs tied. The upper one runs from the line through a diode and has 50 Ω in its ground lead, so its output sits near 5.2 V and it carries the load while the line is present. The line also charges a 6.5 V battery through a diode and a resistor chosen for the charge rate; the lower regulator runs from the battery and holds the output at 5 V when the line is gone. The diodes stop either source feeding back into the other.
notes: Output 5.2 V on line power, 5 V on battery.

circuits.title: Ripple rejection enhancement
circuits.description: The 5 V adjustable circuit (121 Ω / 365 Ω, 1 %) with a 10 µF capacitor, C1, from ADJ to ground. C1 keeps ripple out of the feedback path; its reactance at the ripple frequency should be about equal to R1. Input 6.5 V or more with 10 µF; 150 µF at the output.
notes: VIN ≥ 6.5 V; VOUT = 5 V.

circuits.title: Automatic light control
circuits.description: The adjustable part with 1.2 kΩ from OUTPUT to ADJ and a phototransistor from ADJ to ground, driving a lamp at the output. In light the phototransistor conducts and grounds ADJ, so the lamp stays off; in the dark it turns off, the regulator holds 1.25 V from OUTPUT to ADJ and the lamp lights. 10 µF at the input, 100 µF at the output.

circuits.title: Negative supply from a fixed regulator
circuits.description: A floating transformer winding and bridge rectifier charge a 10,000 µF reservoir that feeds a fixed-output part. Its OUTPUT is tied to system ground, so the GND pin and the rectifier's negative side sit below ground, giving −12 V for an op amp or other negative rail. 100 µF across the output.
notes: The transformer secondary floats; VOUT = −12 V.

circuits.title: Remote sensing
circuits.description: The adjustable part set to 5 V by 121 Ω and 365 Ω, feeding a load RL through line resistance Rp (300 mV drop at most). An LM301A wired as a voltage follower takes the load voltage through 1 kΩ at its non-inverting input and drives the top of the 121 Ω resistor through 25 Ω, so the output is corrected for the drop in Rp without loading the output. The bottom of the divider and the op amp's negative supply return through 25 Ω, bypassed by 5 µF, to the load return. 10 µF at the input, 100 µF at the output, 100 pF compensation on the LM301A.
notes: LM301A pin numbers: 1 COMP1, 2 IN−, 3 IN+, 4 V−, 6 OUT, 7 V+, 8 COMP2.

operation.text: Three versions: fixed 3.3 V, fixed 5.0 V and adjustable. The fixed versions carry the setting resistors inside, with pin 1 as ground; the adjustable version needs two outside resistors and pin 1 is ADJ. The pin order is that of the LM317. The LM1085 (3 A) and LM1086 (1.5 A) are the lower-current members of the family.

The loop is built like the LM317's, but the pass element is a single NPN transistor rather than a Darlington, which removes one base-emitter drop from the dropout. This quasi-LDO structure draws less quiescent current than a PNP LDO. Dropout is at most 1.5 V at full load over temperature.
On chip: a band-gap reference trimmed with zeners, a current limit and a thermal shutdown.

Rejection comes from the open-loop gain of the feedback loop and is 75 dB typical. When the adjustable part is set above VREF the rejection drops by the closed-loop gain VO/VREF: a 5 V setting loses a factor of four, 12 dB. A capacitor from ADJ to ground, with an impedance no higher than R1 at the ripple frequency, stops the ripple being amplified and wins the loss back.

The part regulates the voltage between OUTPUT and its GND or ADJ pin, so drops in the wiring to a remote load add to the load error. For a fixed part, the load's leads should go directly to OUTPUT and to the GND pin. For the adjustable part, the top of R1 should be wired at OUTPUT, not at the load; the bottom of R2 can be returned at the load's ground to sense the ground drop.

The current limit folds back as the input-to-output differential rises (see the short-circuit current curve). At normal start-up the output follows the input and the differential stays small, but after a short the differential is large, and the limit can be slow to recover; if the limited current cannot raise the output, the output may settle at a low level. Cycling the input power restores normal start-up.

The adjustable part holds 1.25 V (VREF) from OUTPUT to ADJ. With R1 across that voltage the resulting current flows through R2, and its drop adds to VREF. The ADJ current (120 µA max) adds a small error that is negligible with R1 near 100 Ω. In the fixed parts R1 and R2 are internal.
The adjustable part needs a load current of at least 10 mA (5 mA typical, at VIN − VOUT = 25 V) to stay in regulation; the current through R1 counts toward it.

The loop needs some series resistance in the output capacitor: the ESR of a solid tantalum or aluminium electrolytic places a zero near 500 kHz that adds phase margin. Aluminium electrolytic ESR rises steeply in the cold, so transient response over temperature needs checking; tantalum ESR changes by less than 2:1 over temperature. 10 µF tantalum or 50 µF aluminium suits most uses. With a capacitor on ADJ, raise the output capacitor to 22 µF tantalum or 150 µF aluminium. The input and ADJ capacitors may be of other types; 10 µF is a reasonable input value.

Loads with large current steps, such as processors, benefit from more output capacitance and lower ESR, since the output steps by ΔI × ESR; paralleling tantalum and ceramic parts lowers the total ESR. Output capacitance may be increased without limit; it improves transient response and stability.

Normally no protection diode is needed. On the adjustable part the internal resistance between ADJ and OUTPUT limits the current, even with a capacitor on ADJ, and ADJ withstands ±25 V transients relative to the output. A shorted input lets the output capacitor discharge back into OUTPUT; the internal diode from OUTPUT to INPUT takes surges of 10 A to 20 A lasting microseconds. With a very large output capacitor (≥ 1000 µF) and an input shorted instantly to ground the part can be damaged, and an external diode from OUTPUT to INPUT is recommended.
A fixed resistor from ADJ to OUTPUT makes the part a precision current regulator. Bypassing ADJ gives ripple rejection higher than plain three-terminal regulators reach.
The input supply should be well regulated, below the maximum input-to-output differential, and above the output by the dropout voltage with margin to spare. 10 µF or more at the input bypasses noise.

Keep all the parts on one side of the board, close to the regulator pins, with short, wide traces; trace width and copper weight follow from the current and the heat to be spread. A field of plated vias in the pad under the tab carries heat to inner planes or a bottom copper plane. A TO-263 layout: input capacitor C1 on the input rail on one side of U1, output capacitor C2 on the output rail on the other, R1 and R2 beside the ADJ/GND pin with a feedback ground, the tab pad on the output.

The chip has two thermal sections with separate limits: the control section at TJ(max) 125 °C and the output section at 150 °C, each with its own junction-to-case resistance. Work out θJA(max) and then θHA(max) for each and use the lower θHA(max) to pick the heat sink. θCH is about 0.2 °C/W with thermal compound and 0 °C/W with the case soldered to the sink. For PCB copper used as the sink, the copper area follows from the heat sink resistance curve.
Regulation figures hold up to 30 W dissipation, which is available only over part of the input-to-output range; the current limit falls as the differential rises.
